report.source_text: After discontinuing antihistamines for 1 week, a water provocation test was administered. This involved regional contact using a damp cloth on the patient’s trunk, maintained at 35°C (figure 1A). After 20 min, there was a development of urticarial eruption on the trunk, which was consistent with the patient’s natural exposure to water (figure 1B).

report.source_text: On evaluation at our clinic, cetirizine, a second-generation H1 antihistamine, was prescribed at 10 mg daily, leading to further symptom relief. Following this, the use of montelukast was discontinued, and the patient continued to experience substantial relief from the wheals.

clinician.trajectory_summary: An adolescent girl presented with a 2-year history of pinpoint wheals with erythematous flares occurring immediately after water exposure regardless of source or temperature, lasting 30–60 minutes and resolving spontaneously. Physical examination showed clear skin without dermographism. Routine labs including CBC, liver and renal function, immunoglobulin panels, and thyroid tests were normal. A controlled water provocation test at 35°C induced a urticarial eruption on the trunk after 20 minutes, reproducing the patient's natural symptoms. No other inducible urticarias provocation tests were reported. Treatment with cetirizine led to symptom relief. These findings support the diagnosis of aquagenic urticaria.
